Description: The study of accounting provides a language for communicating financial information and for making a variety of decisions. These decisions range from a simple evaluation of the creditworthiness of a potential customer to a complex analysis of a firm facing financial distress. In addition to a set of core courses, the accounting concentration offers a wide array of courses. This curriculum prepares students for a variety of careers. The courses in financial accounting are important for those planning careers as financial analysts, investment bankers, and managers. In each of these roles, an individual must be able to understand how a firm's performance and position is reported and how that information is used by market participants in the valuation of the firm. The courses in managerial accounting prepare students for careers in consulting and the management of manufacturing or service organizations. There is a great deal of flexibility in the accounting concentration, so a student can select those courses that best suit their interests and career plans. A student who chooses to concentrate in accounting can select courses that develop the following skills and knowledge bases: a language of business; an understanding of how accounting information is used in the securities market and in contracting; an understanding of the incentives for and the consequences of earnings management; a framework for financial statement analysis; a framework for structuring a firm’s system of internal controls; a basic understanding of taxes and their effect on business decisions; and an ability to analyze case studies.

[3] Through applied experiences in Chicago and beyond, you'll meet face-to-face with professionals in the field to analyze urgent policy problems and design solutions that work, using the latest science and technology. The core curriculum draws on a variety of disciplines and fields, including economics, sociology, political science, statistics, econometrics, political economy, organizational theory, and program evaluation, an ideal fit for students seeking a multidisciplinary approach to the study of public policy. Description: Anthropology is the intensive study of human diversity across time and space, a field that is both eclectic and rigorous. Methods deployed can include ethnography, linguistics, archaeology, and biology while topics anthropologists study are as varied as human experience. Anthropology is grounded in intensive fieldwork and, as practiced at the University of Chicago, an understanding that cultural realities need to be studied, theorized, and accounted for prior to any attempts to universalize human behavior. Students with training in anthropology are sought after by NGOs, the medical field, market research, museums, education, and government.

Description: Anthropology is the intensive study of human diversity across time and space. It is a field that is both eclectic and rigorous. Anthropologists at the University of Chicago seek to study, theorize, and account for cultural realities, past and present, and the topics they study are as varied as the human experience. The discipline is often grounded in fieldwork and can be informed by ethnography, linguistics, history, archaeology, and biology. At the undergraduate level, courses generally align with one of Anthropology's four traditional subfields: archaeological, biological, linguistic, or sociocultural anthropology. Coursework may be thematic and comparative, topically or regionally focused, and/or emphasize methodological training. Anthropology majors are sought after by NGOs and find careers in medicine, business, technology, museums, education, and government. Students also receive excellent training for continuing graduate study in the social sciences, humanities, or biological fields. [3]

Description: Based in the Department of Art History, the interdisciplinary minor in Architectural Studies (ARCH) equips students to analyze the form and changing history of the built environment through a combination of coursework in architectural history with up to four courses on architectural and urban design topics offered in any department. [2, 6] This is the only University program that focuses on designing and analyzing buildings as material, three-dimensional, culturally meaningful environments. [2, 6] Students may choose to minor in architectural studies because they are interested in analyzing the built environment from a liberal arts perspective or because they are considering applying to architecture school. [2, 6] The minor could complement a major in the social sciences or humanities by exploring the material setting of history and social life or the context for works of literature, film, music, or drama. [3, 6] It could equally complement a major in the sciences, such as medical fields, ecology, geology, physics, or mathematics. [6] The minor degree in Architectural Studies focuses on the built environment from a humanities perspective and requires a total of six courses. [2, 6]

While maintaining the University of Chicago's traditional emphasis on the life of the mind, the major in art history prepares students for advanced study at the graduate level as well as for a wide array of careers involving visual acuity, design, research, and analysis.

Graduates of the Astrophysics program will be positioned to pursue advanced degrees in physics, astronomy, or similar fields, or enter government service, science education, or scientific journalism. [3]

Description: "Big Problems" is an interdisciplinary program at The University of Chicago that offers capstone experiences as electives to third- and fourth-year students in the College. [4] The courses are designed to address matters of global or universal concern that intersect with multiple disciplines. [2, 4] The program emphasizes the process of learning how to creatively confront complex intellectual and pragmatic problems that are wider than a student's specific area of expertise and how to manage the resulting uncertainty. [2, 4] It aims to equip students with the skills to think about and deal with significant, persistent issues of our time. [2, 4] The courses often utilize interdisciplinary team teaching to cross disciplinary and divisional boundaries. [2, 4] On the university's official list of undergraduate programs, "Big Problems" is designated as an "Interdisciplinary Opportunity," not a major or a minor.

Coursework opportunities at the Marine Biological Laboratory are particularly suited for this track. 3) Interdisciplinary Track – Global and Public Health – Provides a cross-cutting education through coursework and research in the biology of disease, as well as economic and social factors influencing health outcomes worldwide.. The minor is built upon a foundation of three core courses: the Autumn Quarter Chicago Studies colloquium (CHST 10000), a faculty-led immersive course during the Winter Quarter, and a Spring research seminar (CHST 20000). To earn the minor, students must also complete three electives and a short experiential learning component. Students may take electives from an approved list of courses that draw on the city of Chicago as an object of study, a site of inquiry, and/or a context for creative work and public engagement. [4]

Applicants can apply using the Common Application or the Coalition Application. Required materials include the application form, a personal essay (referred to as a writing supplement), and official high school transcripts. While not required, applicants have the option to submit a two-minute video profile, which is highly recommended. [1]
Accredidation: The University of Chicago is accredited by the Higher Learning Commission of the North Central Association. [3]

ProgramName: Minor in Cinema and Media Studies
Requirements: To declare the Minor in Cinema and Media Studies, current students must complete a Minor Approval Form and submit it to the department. [2] The academic requirements consist of completing six courses, including specific introductory and history courses, as well as three electives. [2, 5] All courses for the minor must be taken for quality grades and cannot be double-counted with a major or other minor. [2]
Description: The Minor in Cinema and Media Studies requires the completion of six courses, the first of which should be CMST 10100: Introduction to Film. Students should aim to take this course early in their undergraduate career or at the beginning of their minor course of study. It must be taken no later than Spring Quarter of year 3. Courses in the minor may not be double-counted with the student's major(s) or with other minors and may not be counted toward general education requirements. All classes toward the minor must be taken for quality grades, and more than half of the requirements for the minor must be met by registering for courses bearing University of Chicago course numbers.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies
Requirements: Application requirements are not specific to the Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies but apply to all first-year applicants to The University of Chicago College. Applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. This includes the applicant's high school transcript, a school report, and two teacher recommendations. A personal essay via the chosen application platform is required, as are the UChicago Supplement essays. Submission of SAT or ACT scores is optional.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies with a Specialization in Greek and Roman Cultures
Requirements: First-year applicants to the University of Chicago must submit either the Coalition Application or the Common Application. Required components include the application form, a high school transcript, a school report, and two teacher recommendations. The university also has a supplement which includes an extended essay chosen from several prompts and a shorter essay on why the applicant wants to attend UChicago. While interviews are not required, they are offered as an optional way to demonstrate interest. [13]
Description: The University of Chicago does not offer a program with the exact name 'Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies with a Specialization in Greek and Roman Cultures'. However, it does offer a 'BA in Ancient World Studies'. The description for this program is: "Our Modern World has been shaped by the legacy of ancient civilizations. We are indebted to them for our languages, governments, laws, and religions, our art and our architecture, our science, medicine, and philosophy, and so much more. The study of antiquity has always been fundamental to our understanding of the human condition, as many of the structures, values, and institutions that have shaped the history of humanity were formed in this epoch. In Ancient World Studies, a breadth of human experience is available for study. Our Ancient World Studies program unifies disciplinary areas like Classical Studies (for the Greco-Roman world), Near Eastern Studies (for western Asia and Egypt), Ancient Chinese studies, and so on, framing the study of the ancient world around questions of liberty, justice, equity health, race, gender, and the environment, benefiting from new research and scholarship not only in languages, history, and linguistics, but in anthropology, archaeology, art history, economics, political science, sociology, and the natural sciences. Although we call the major “Ancient World Studies,” it should also be noted that part of our field, and in particular part of the existing teaching and research work within our department, involves study of the continuing relevance and legacy of these cultures in the modern world. This can include everything from 18th-century musical settings of first-century Roman lyrics, to movie re-tellings of the Trojan War stories, to games and puzzles built around Egyptian pyramids."

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies with a Specialization in Language and Literature
Description: The major program in Classical Studies offers a Language and Literature variant that combines the reading of Greek and Latin texts with diverse areas of study including art and archaeology, history, philosophy, religion, and science. [2] The overall BA degree in Classical Studies aims to equip students with strong skills in interpretation, writing, critical thinking, close reading, and textual and visual analysis, preparing them for careers in fields like teaching, scholarly research, law, and publishing. [2]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies with a Specialization in Language Intensive
Requirements: Application for admission is made to The College of the University of Chicago, not to a specific major. First-year applicants must submit either the Coalition Application or the Common Application, the UChicago Supplement, which includes a 'Why Us?' essay and an extended essay from a choice of prompts, two teacher recommendations, and a high school transcript. An application fee or a fee waiver is also required. The university has a test-optional policy regarding SAT/ACT scores.

ProgramName: Minor in Classical Studies
Description: The minor in Classical Studies requires a total of six courses in Greek (GREK), Latin (LATN), or Classical Civilization (CLCV). [7] Of these six courses: Only three of these courses may be elementary language courses (e.g. GREK 10100-10200-10300). [7] CLCV courses (1) may not be double counted with the student's major(s) or with other minors and (2) may not be counted toward general education requirements. [7] Our undergraduate minors all attain some expertise in chosen areas of classical civilization, and many also choose to study Greek, Latin, or both. [7] The linguistic, interpretive, critical, and analytical skills gained by our minors, along with their understanding of the classical world, equip them well both for their programs of study in their majors and for a wide variety of careers. [7]
ScholarshipType: The University of Chicago offers need-based scholarships and grants, which are referred to as gift aid and do not need to be repaid. [8] The university also has merit-based scholarships available. [8] Students may also be eligible for federal and state grants, as well as student employment opportunities. [8, 15]

ProgramName: Minor in Climate and Sustainable Growth
Requirements: The minor in Climate and Sustainable Growth consists of six courses: two mandatory courses and a choice of four other courses drawn from the foundational courses from the major. The two mandatory courses are (i) CCSG 19000 The Climate and Growth Challenge and (ii) CCSG 20500 Energy: Science, Technology, and Human Usage. [2, 8, 9] Because courses for the minor may overlap with courses a student is taking for their major, they must have approval from the Director of Undergraduate Studies for the set of courses used for the minor. [2] Courses in the minor must be taken for quality grades and may not be double-counted with the student's major(s), other minors, or general education requirements. [9]
Description: Climate change is one of the central challenges facing humanity. Increasing temperatures due to CO2 emissions, by changing ecosystems, weather patterns, sea levels, among other harms, threatens humans and other living things. Meeting this challenge entails transforming the global energy system to eliminate carbon emissions from fossil fuels. At the same time, energy poverty is still common in many parts of the world. Allowing people in those parts of the world to flourish and develop, as is their right, requires increasing energy access while the energy system is transformed, creating a double challenge. [4] The minor in Climate and Sustainable Growth consists of six courses: two mandatory courses and a choice of four other courses drawn from the foundational courses from the major. [3, 4] The two mandatory courses are (i) CCSG 19000 The Climate and Growth Challenge and (ii) CCSG 20500 Energy: Science, Technology, and Human Usage. [3, 4] Using a 360-degree approach, the program provides students with a foundational understanding of the climate and growth challenge. [2]

ProgramName: Minor in Clinical and Translational Science
Description: The minor in Clinical and Translational Science provides students with the foundational skills, methodology, and principles of high-quality, responsible clinical and translational research. Students will be exposed to the ways in which clinical and translational research is operationalized from the bench to the bedside, and to the community. In addition to a core curriculum, students in the minor will have an opportunity to participate in a clinical research experience.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Cognitive Science
Requirements: Application for admission to The University of Chicago is made through the Common Application or the Coalition Application. There are no specific application requirements for the Bachelor of Arts in Cognitive Science beyond the general requirements for undergraduate admission. Students apply to the university as a whole and can declare their major later. The application includes a university-specific supplement with essays.
Description: Cognitive science explores the nature of cognitive processes telles que la perception, le raisonnement, la mémoire, l'attention, le langage, la prise de décision, l'émotion, le contrôle moteur et la résolution de problèmes. Le but de la science cognitive, énoncé simplement, est de comprendre comment fonctionne l'esprit, chez les humains, les animaux et les machines. La science cognitive a émergé dans la dernière partie du 20e siècle à l'intersection de l'informatique, de la linguistique, des neurosciences, de la philosophie et de la psychologie, et est une entreprise intrinsèquement interdisciplinaire, s'appuyant sur des outils et des idées des sciences sociales, des sciences physiques et biologiques, et les sciences humaines. Les sujets de recherche incluent (mais ne sont pas limités à) le développement cognitif, le traitement cognitif, le jugement et la prise de décision, le langage et la communication, les bases neurologiques de la cognition, de la perception et de la mémoire, la philosophie de l'esprit et l'intelligence artificielle. Une caractéristique déterminante de la science cognitive est son accent sur l'intégration entre les domaines, pour une étude véritablement interdisciplinaire de l'esprit.
AverageScholarshipAmount: 52% of freshmen at University of Chicago receive an institutional scholarship of approximately $45,686 on average. [6]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit awards start at $2,000. [10]
ScholarshipType: Merit-based scholarships, need-based scholarships such as the Odyssey Scholarship Program, First Phoenix Scholarship for first-generation students, and others. [10, 14]

ProgramName: Minor in Cognitive Science
Description: Cognitive science explores the nature of cognitive processes such as perception, reasoning, memory, attention, language, decision making, emotion, motor control, and problem solving. The goal of cognitive science, stated simply, is to understand how minds work, in humans, animals, and machines. Cognitive science emerged in the latter part of the 20th century at the intersection of computer science, linguistics, neuroscience, philosophy, and psychology, an an is inherently in interdisciplinary an an endeavor, drawing on tools and ideas from the social sciences, the physical and biological sciences, and the humanities. Topics of research include (but are not limited to) cognitive development, cognitive processing, judgment and decision making, language and communication, the neurological bases of cognition, perception, and memory, philosophy of mind, and artificial intelligence. A defining feature of cognitive science is its emphasis on integration among fields, for a truly interdisciplinary study of the mind. Students will be trained in formal methods of analysis and modeling that are common in majors in the physical and biological sciences, but often absent from majors in the humanities and social sciences; at the same time, students will also be trained in the advanced reasoning skills that define humanistic inquiry, but are often absent from more technical or applied majors. The undergraduate major in Cognitive Science at the University of Chicago is designed to embody this interdisciplinary approach to the study of the mind and brain.
ScholarshipAmount: Merit awards start at $2,000; some full-tuition scholarships are available. [19, 20]
ScholarshipType: Merit-based, need-based, and scholarships for specific groups like first-generation students or children of police and firefighters. [8, 12, 20]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Human Development
Department: The College, Division of the Social Sciences
Description: The undergraduate program in Comparative Human Development (CHDV) focuses on the study of persons over the course of life; on the social, cultural, biological, and psychological processes that jointly influence development; and on growth over time in different social and cultural settings. [2] The study of human development also offers a unique lens through which we consider broad questions relevant to the social sciences, like the processes and impacts of social change, and the interactions of biology and culture. [2] Given this interdisciplinary scope, the program in Comparative Human Development provides an excellent preparation for students interested in advanced postgraduate study at the frontiers of several social science disciplines, or in careers and professions that require a broad and integrated understanding of human experience and behavior—e.g., mental health, education, social work, health care, or human resource and organizational work in community or corporate settings. [2]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Literature
Requirements: Applicants must submit either the Coalition Application or the Common Application. All applicants must also complete the UChicago Supplement, which includes a short essay on why they wish to attend the University of Chicago and one extended essay chosen from a list of prompts. [3] Other required materials include a school report and two teacher recommendations. [3]
Description: TThe undergraduate program is designed for students who wish to pursue an interdisciplinary course of study focused on literature in various languages and from different parts of the world. Students can come from diverse backgrounds, whether they have strong skills in languages other than English or a keen interest in literary studies that cross national boundaries. The program is also suited for those wanting to explore the relationship between literature and culture in depth. Each student collaborates with the Director of Undergraduate Studies (DUS) to create a personalized course plan. The major consists of seven courses in a primary and secondary field, a foundational course in comparative literary theory, two additional courses in literary theory or methods, and a capstone BA project workshop. [4]

ProgramName: Minor in Comparative Literature
Requirements: General application requirements are not specified at the institute level. Applicants should refer to the specific requirements for undergraduate or graduate admissions.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies
Requirements: Application requirements are not specific to the Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies, but are for general admission to The College at the University of Chicago. Applicants must submit a Common Application or Coalition Application, a school report, transcripts, and teacher recommendations. The application also includes a required University of Chicago Supplement, which features extended essay questions. A two-minute video introduction is an optional component for all applicants.

Description: The BA program in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies offers an interdisciplinary curriculum through which students can examine the histories, languages, and cultures of the racial and ethnic groups in and of themselves, in relationship to each other, and, particularly, in structural contexts of power. [1] A degree in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies offers training designed to impart fundamental skills in critical thinking, comparative analysis, social theory, research methods, and written expression. [1] A student who obtains a BA in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies will be well prepared for admission to graduate programs in the humanities and social sciences, to professional schools in law, medicine, public health, social work, business, or international affairs, and to careers in education, journalism, politics, creative writing, and the nonprofit sector. [1]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit scholarships start at $2,000; some scholarships offer full tuition.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies with a Specialization in Africa Past and Present
Requirements: Beyond your transcript and teacher/counselor recommendations, you can also submit supplemental application materials. The Coalition Application and Common Application allow you to submit a wide variety of materials, including but not limited to, a resume, a creative writing sample or research abstract, or a graded paper. In addition to these materials, you can also consider submitting a two-minute video introduction in lieu of a traditional college interview. The video introduction is a fun and easy way for you to show us who you are and why you’re interested in UChicago—in your own voice, and on your own time. The video is completely optional, and you will not be penalized if you choose not to submit one.
Description: The BA program in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies offers an interdisciplinary curriculum through which students can examine the histories, languages, and cultures of the racial and ethnic groups in and of themselves, in relationship to each other, and, particularly, in structural contexts of power. [3] Focusing on genocide, slavery, conquest, confinement, immigration, and the diaspora of peoples around the globe, Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies examines the material, artistic, and literary expressions of peoples who originated in Africa, Latin America, Asia, and Europe, who moved voluntarily or were forcefully bound over to the Americas and here evolved stigmatized identities, which were tied to the cultures and histories of their natal lands in complicated ways. [3] A student who obtains a BA in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies will be well prepared for admission to graduate programs in the humanities and social sciences, to professional schools in law, medicine, public health, social work, business, or international affairs, and to careers in education, journalism, politics, creative writing, and the nonprofit sector. [3] A degree in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies offers training designed to impart fundamental skills in critical thinking, comparative analysis, social theory, research methods, and written expression. [3]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies with a Specialization in African American Studies
Requirements: General application requirements for undergraduate admission to The University of Chicago include the Common Application or Coalition Application, responses to the UChicago Supplement essays, two teacher recommendations, and a secondary school report with a transcript. [7, 12] Submission of SAT or ACT scores is optional. [7]
ScholarshipType: The University of Chicago offers merit-based and need-based scholarships. [2] All first-year applicants are automatically considered for available merit scholarships, which are awarded based on academic and extracurricular achievements, leadership, and community commitment. [4] Scholarship amounts start at $2,000 and can be for four years or for summer opportunities. [4] Specific scholarships include the University Scholarship, the Chicago Public Schools Scholarship (up to full-tuition), and the First Phoenix Scholarship for first-generation students ($20,000 over four years). [2, 3, 4]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies with a Specialization in Asian American Studies
Requirements: Application requirements for undergraduate admission to The University of Chicago are not specific to the major. All applicants must submit a complete application, which includes essays (the UChicago Supplement, known as the "Uncommon Essay," is a distinctive feature), official transcripts, and two teacher recommendations. [5, 8] The submission of standardized test scores is optional. [7]
Description: The BA program in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies offers an interdisciplinary curriculum through which students can examine the histories, languages, and cultures of the racial and ethnic groups in and of themselves, in relationship to each other, and, particularly, in structural contexts of power. A student who obtains a BA in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies will be well prepared for admission to graduate programs in the humanities and social sciences, to professional schools in law, medicine, public health, social work, business, or international affairs, and to careers in education, journalism, politics, creative writing, and the nonprofit sector. A degree in Comparative Race and Ethnic Studies offers training designed to impart fundamental skills in critical thinking, comparative analysis, social theory, research methods, and written expression. Areas of specialization include: Africa Past and Present, African American Studies, Latino/a Studies, Asian American Studies, and Native American Studies. This major/minor is also available to students interested in the study of Africa in a comparative framework. [6]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Computational and Applied Mathematics
Description: The Departments of Computer Science, Mathematics, and Statistics offer a BS in Computational and Applied Mathematics. The program is designed for students who intend to specialize in computational and/or applied mathematics, as well as students who want to acquire a strong quantitative background to be applied in such varied areas as physics, biological sciences, engineering, operations research, economics, and finance. [1]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts/Master of Science in Computational Analysis and Public Policy
Minor in Computational Neuroscience
Description: The Minor in Computational Neuroscience (CNS) is intended for both Neuroscience Majors and Non-Majors. [2] It provides students with a strong foundation in the mathematical and computational approaches used to study the brain. [2] Computational neuroscience integrates methods from mathematics, statistics, computer science, and physics to model neural systems, analyze complex datasets, and uncover the principles underlying brain function. [2] Pursuing this minor equips students with quantitative skills essential for modern neuroscience, including computational modeling, neural data analysis, and theoretical frameworks. [2] For neuroscience majors, it provides the analytical tools needed to interpret data, test hypotheses, and bridge the gap between theory and experiment. [2] For non-neuroscience majors, the minor offers an opportunity to apply quantitative training to one of the most compelling problems in science—understanding how the brain works. [2] These tools prepare students for careers in neuroscience, biomedical engineering, artificial intelligence, and other quantitative fields. [2]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts/Master of Arts in Computational Social Science
Description: The University of Chicago offers joint BA/MA programs that allow qualified students to begin a graduate course of study while completing their undergraduate work in the College. [4] Applicants for these programs, including the pathway for the Master's in Computational Social Science, must have completed a significant part of their undergraduate program before applying. [4] Typically, students are admitted to candidacy for the master's degree during their fourth year in the College, during which they are billed for tuition at the graduate rate. [4] Interested students are advised to discuss their plans with their College adviser early, aiming to complete general education requirements by the end of their second year and meeting with their adviser in the Autumn Quarter of their third year. [4] Students earn their BA at the end of the fourth year and the master's degree at the end of the fifth year. [1]

ProgramName: Minor in Computational Social Science
Requirements: The minor consists of six courses: one course introducing contemporary approaches for performing Computational Social Science research, one data analysis course, two computational methods courses, and two electives in Computational Social Science. [2, 3] Courses in the minor must be taken for quality grades and may not be double counted with the student's major(s), other minors, or general education requirements. [2, 3] Students who wish to declare a minor in Computational Social Science must reach out to the Associate Director for Undergraduate Studies to indicate their intention to complete the minor and have their Consent to Complete a Minor Program form signed. [2, 3] Students will need to submit the signed form to their College Adviser before the end of the Spring Quarter of their third year. [2, 3]
Department: The College, Division of Social Sciences
Description: Computational Social Science is an emergent field at the intersection of the social and computational sciences—leveraging computational advances, such as those in AI and machine learning, as well as the widespread availability of “big data,” to drive the next generation of social research. [2, 5] The Minor in Computational Social Science enables students in the social sciences to build fundamental computational skills with the purpose of enriching existing approaches to social scientific inquiry. [2, 5] Additionally, for students outside of the social sciences (e.g., in the physical and biological sciences), it provides an opportunity to consolidate their computational, mathematical, and statistical skills, as well as apply these skills to questions about social and cultural life. [2, 5] Over the course of the program, students will learn how computational approaches complement and expand upon traditional research designs in the social sciences, as well as gain the hands-on computer programming and data analysis skills necessary to implement these computationally enhanced research designs. [2, 3, 5] For instance, students will learn how “big data” and AI technologies enhance traditional observational studies and explore simulation-based research designs, as well as investigate how to run large, computationally enhanced surveys and digital experiments. [2, 3, 5] They will additionally have the opportunity to explore advanced approaches for applying their computational and analytical skills to social science problems in elective courses in Computational Social Science. [3, 5] For example, students may complete machine learning and high-performance computing coursework, with an emphasis on applicability to social scientific research. [3, 5]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Computer Science
Requirements: The University of Chicago accepts the Common Application and the Coalition Application. First-year applicants must submit the application, a supplemental essay, high school transcript, and two teacher recommendations. Providing a portfolio of supplementary material is optional.
Description: The computer science program offers both BA and BS degrees. Students who earn the BA degree study a breadth of foundational computer science topics and are prepared for either graduate study in computer science or a career in industry. A computer science major also serves as an excellent foundation for work in other areas, including but not limited to mathematics, the natural sciences, social sciences, public administration, and the arts. [11, 22]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Computer Science
Requirements: Application to the undergraduate program at the University of Chicago is handled through the general admissions process for The College, not by individual departments. Applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application, along with the UChicago Supplement, which includes a 'Why Us?' essay and an extended essay from a choice of creative prompts. [13, 16] Additional requirements include a high school transcript and two teacher recommendations. [13, 14] An optional two-minute video introduction may also be submitted. [6] The university does not specify minimum GPA requirements but notes that the majority of enrolled first-year students have a GPA of 3.75 or higher. [21]
Description: The computer science program at the University of Chicago offers both BA and BS degrees. The Bachelor of Science (BS) in Computer Science is designed to prepare students with a depth of foundational knowledge in the field. Students pursuing the BS degree are required to complete a three-course specialization. As of the 2024-25 academic year, the BS requirements include a four-course introductory sequence, a three-course Theory sequence, a one-course Systems requirement, a three-course specialization, and three electives.
ScholarshipType: Merit-based, Need-based, a combination of both

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts/Master of Science in Computer Science
Requirements: The Bachelor of Arts/Master of Science in Computer Science is a joint degree program open to current, outstanding undergraduate students at the University of Chicago. [8, 9] Students must be on track to complete their undergraduate requirements by the end of their third year, as the fourth year is focused on graduate-level requirements. [8] Admission to the MS portion of the program is not automatic; students must apply and be admitted to the joint MS program. [7, 11] Applications are submitted through the Physical Sciences Division (PSD) graduate application site during the student's fourth year. [8]
Department: The College; Department of Computer Science
Concentration: The Computer Science Department offers three options for the joint BA/MS and BS/MS degrees: a research-oriented option for Computer Science majors, a professionally-oriented option for Computer Science majors, and a professionally-oriented option for non-CS majors.
Description: Outstanding undergraduates may apply to complete an MS in computer science along with a BA or BS (generalized to "Bx") during their four years at the College. Students must be admitted to the joint MS program. There are three different paths to a Bx/MS: a research-oriented program for computer science majors (Option 1), a professionally oriented program for computer science majors (Option 2), and a professionally oriented program for non-majors (Option 3). Participants in the Bx/MS program must meet the requirements for the BA or BS, complete nine courses for the MS, and, if applicable, a master's project. Students may double-count up to two courses toward both their Bx and MS degrees.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science/Master of Science in Computer Science
Requirements: The joint Bx/MS program is only open to outstanding University of Chicago undergraduates who are on track to complete their BA/BS requirements by the end of their third year, with at most, 2-3 undergraduate courses left to complete during their fourth year. [7] Students apply to start the Bx/MS program in either the Autumn Quarter of their fourth year or the Winter Quarter of their fourth year. [7] Applications are submitted through the Physical Sciences Division (PSD) graduate application site. [7]

ProgramName: Minor in Computer Science
Requirements: The minor in Computer Science requires a total of six courses. Students must take CMSC 14100 Computer Science with Applications 1 and CMSC 14200 Computer Science with Applications 2 (or a placement exam). The remaining four courses are CMSC electives, with at least two of them being at the 20000-level or above. All courses for the minor must be taken for a quality grade.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Creative Writing
Requirements: Applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, the UChicago Supplement (which includes the "Uncommon Essay"), a Secondary School Report and transcript, and two teacher recommendations. All application materials are submitted online.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts/Master of Arts from the Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice
Requirements: Qualified University of Chicago students in The College apply to the program. Students will need a GPA of 3.25 or higher and should consult with their College adviser and with the admissions office at the Crown Family School as soon as their first year, but no later than early in their third year. [2]
Department: Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice
Fees: The undergraduate tuition for the 2025-2026 academic year is $71,325. [2, 5] The graduate tuition for the Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice for the 2025-2026 academic year is $53,271 for the full-time A.M. program. [4]
Description: The Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice offers students an opportunity to begin their professional training in social work, policy, and social administration while still in the College. [5] At the Crown Family School, we challenge our students to dig deeper to understand the root causes and human costs of social problems. [5] Our community of faculty, alumni, and students is proactive. [5] We reach beyond easy explanations and standard responses. [5] The joint BA/MA program allows qualified students to earn a Bachelor of Arts from the College and a Master of Arts from the Crown Family School in a total of five years. [5, 6]
Accredidation: The Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice master's program has been accredited by the Council on Social Work Education and its predecessor organizations since 1919. [2, 3]
CostPerCredit: $5,919/course for the graduate portion of the program (2025-2026).

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Data Science
Requirements: The University of Chicago requires first-year applicants to submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. In addition to the application itself, students must submit two supplemental essays. The first is a response to a prompt about why the applicant wants to attend the University of Chicago. The second is a response to one of several creative prompts. Other required materials include a high school transcript and two teacher recommendations. [13]
Description: Transdisciplinary by nature, Data Science draws on numerous fields including statistics, computer science and applied mathematics, and also incorporates topics in privacy and ethics, philosophy of science, and economics to better understand the impact of data on society. Therefore, the Data Science curriculum combines computational and analytical skills, extensive knowledge in the domain of application, communication skills, and an emphasis on ethical considerations. The program for the BA in Data Science consists of 15 courses (1500 units) beyond the general education requirement. The standard curriculum includes an introductory sequence to Data Science and programming, an introductory sequence to mathematical methods, and courses on ethics in data science, data visualization, and modeling and machine learning. In addition, the curriculum includes exposure to real-world projects through the Data Science Clinic and three electives. The BA track is recommended for students who would like to combine a Data Science major with another minor or major program. Students interested in mathematically advanced courses and/or graduate research in Data Science can choose the Theory Track, where four MATH and STAT courses replace the mathematical methods sequence.

ProgramName: Minor in Data Science
Minor in Democracy Studies
Department: Social Sciences Collegiate Division, The College
Description: The University of Chicago's Minor in Democracy Studies provides students essential knowledge, insights, methods, and critical perspectives necessary to understanding the world around us and the historical developments that have placed it in such a precarious state. [1, 2] Students in the minor learn, among other topics, how democracy extends well beyond the political arena, to encompass a broad set of structures, including civic organizations, laws, deliberative practices, rhetorical strategies, cultural forms, collective imaginaries, and moral, ethical, and spiritual codes. [1, 5] The minor therefore offers a broad range of courses allowing students to select cross-disciplinary electives suitable to forming a broadly conceived program of study. [1, 5] Students in the minor complete a total of five courses, including one required course, “DEMS 15000: Democracy and Its Critics,” and four electives. [1, 2, 5]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts/Master of Arts in Digital Studies of Language, Culture, and History

ScholarshipAmount: Applicants may be awarded a $12,000 merit-based Division of the Arts & Humanities Scholarship, a $22,500 merit-based Dean's Scholarship, a $10,000 Liberal Arts Alumni Scholarship, a $10,000 Illinois Resident Scholarship, or a $10,000 Educational Access Scholarship. [10]
ScholarshipType: Merit-based, alumni-based, residency-based, and need-based (based on Pell Grant eligibility). [10]

ProgramName: Minor in Digital Studies of Language, Culture, and History
Requirements: To complete the Minor in Digital Studies of Language, Culture, and History, students must be enrolled at the University of Chicago and take six specific courses. [1] There is no information on the official university website about a separate application process to declare the minor.
Department: The College of the University of Chicago
Description: The minor in Digital Studies of Language, Culture, and History introduces students to computer programming and the use of cutting-edge software tools for representing, exploring, analyzing, and publishing the products of human language and culture. [1] These products range from everyday speech and writing to historical documents and literary texts, and they encompass music and art as well as mundane objects, places, and institutions. [1] The courses in this minor will help students not just to understand and use digital tools but to see digital computing as a cultural activity in its own right—an activity to be studied with respect to its historical development, social setting, cultural impact, and aesthetic qualities, as well as the ethical problems it creates in our increasingly digitized and networked world. [1] This minor does not require a background in mathematics or computing but is designed for students who are majoring in the humanities or humanistic social sciences. [1]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit awards start at $2,000

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in East Asian Languages and Civilizations

Description: The Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations (EALC) offers a BA program in East Asian studies that introduces students to the traditional and modern civilizations of China, Japan, and Korea, and provides them with the opportunity to achieve a basic reading and speaking knowledge of Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. [1, 5] This program is interdisciplinary, and students may take relevant courses in both the humanities and the social sciences. [1, 5] Students in other fields of study may also complete a minor in EALC. [1, 5]

Description: The Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations (EALC) offers a BA program in East Asian studies that introduces students to the traditional and modern civilizations of China, Japan, and Korea, and provides them with the opportunity to achieve a basic reading and speaking knowledge of Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. [4] This program is interdisciplinary, and students may take relevant courses in both the humanities and the social sciences. [4]

Description: The Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations (EALC) offers a BA program in East Asian studies that introduces students to the traditional and modern civilizations of China, Japan, and Korea, and provides them with the opportunity to achieve a basic reading and speaking knowledge of Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Economics
Bachelor of Arts in Economics with a Specialization in Business Economics
Department: Kenneth C. Griffin Department of Economics
Description: The specialization in business economics is organized around the fundamental economic theory and empirical methods that students interested in pursuing careers in the private sector, the non-profit sector, and the public sector (among others) will find useful. Students who begin by following the standard economics major path have several decision points at which they can choose to specialize in business economics. Students should consult early in the first year with the Department of Economics Undergraduate Program to design a curriculum that satisfies their professional goals. [8]
ScholarshipType: Need-based and merit-based scholarships are available. [4, 14, 16, 17, 18, 21, 22, 28]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Economics with a Specialization in Data Science
Requirements: Applicants must submit their application through the Common Application or Coalition Application. The application includes the University of Chicago's specific essay questions, known for their unique and thought-provoking prompts. [13, 18] Other required documents include high school transcripts and letters of recommendation. [2, 5] The university values intellectual curiosity and a passion for learning. [2]
Department: The College, Kenneth C. Griffin Department of Economics
Description: Broadly, economics studies how society allocates scarce resources. Our program, which spans principles to advanced topics classes, from preparatory courses in mathematics and statistics to research opportunities, trains students to reason like economists, construct and analyze models, and compare model predictions to real-world observations. Upon completing the major, we expect students to achieve the following learning outcomes: (1) Analytical Reasoning: Students will develop strong analytical reasoning abilities. They will be able to apply logical and quantitative tools to analyze theoretical and empirical problems in economics. (2) Core Knowledge: Students will learn and be able to apply core economic concepts in microeconomics and macroeconomics. (3) Data Analysis Skills: Students will be able to analyze data using statistical software. (4) Critical Thinking: Students will be able to evaluate the validity of theoretical arguments and empirical results. (5) Communication Skills: Students will be able to clearly and effectively communicate economic arguments.
ScholarshipType: Need-based and merit-based scholarships are available.

ProgramName: Minor in Economics
ScholarshipType: The University of Chicago offers a 'No-Loan' policy, replacing need-based loans with grants and scholarships for all admitted undergraduate students with demonstrated financial need.

ProgramName: Minor in Education and Society
Requirements: To declare the Minor in Education and Society, students must complete an EDSO Declaration Form and send it to the Director of Instructional Programs before the end of the Spring Quarter of their third year. [6] The minor requires the completion of five courses in total: one required course (CHDV 20100 Human Development Research Design) and four approved electives. [2, 6] Courses for the minor cannot be double-counted with a major or other requirements and must be taken for quality grades. [2]
Description: Courses in the Education and Society minor probe fundamental questions about the interplay between human development and the institution of schooling using the tools of the social science disciplines. [4, 5] Courses explore how people learn and teach as well as the complex relationships between education and the communities and societies it is situated within. [4, 5] Courses are theory-driven yet also provide important insights into the social contexts of education, strategies for strengthening educational practice, and levers for reducing social inequality in academic achievement. [4, 5] The minor spans a diverse set of course listings because education as a discipline spans the life course and happens in many contexts: in the schoolhouse, the family, communities, workplaces, and political arenas. [4] Psychological, social, economic, political, and cultural factors influence educational trajectories and outcomes ranging from individual health and income to forms of social inequality and trajectories of economic development. [4, 5] The interactions among educational organizations and other institutions shape the possibilities for innovation and intentional reform. To understand the intersection of educational institutions and the broader societies, these courses cross boundaries among theory, research, policy, and practice. [4] This minor is focused on education topics from a theoretical and methodological perspective. [4, 5] College students in any field of study may complete a minor in Education and Society. [4] The flexibility of this course of study complements majors in any of the disciplines. [4, 5]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in English Language and Literature
Requirements: Prospective students apply to The University of Chicago's College, not to a specific major. Declaration of a major in English Language and Literature occurs after matriculation. General application requirements include the Common Application or Coalition Application, essays, and recommendations. No additional requirements are specified for the English Language and Literature program.

ProgramName: Minor in English Language and Literature
Bachelor of Arts in Environment, Geography, and Urbanization
Requirements: Application to the Bachelor of Arts in Environment, Geography, and Urbanization is done through the general undergraduate admissions process for The University of Chicago. There are no specific additional application requirements for this major. The general application requirements include the application form, a high school transcript, and letters of recommendation. Submission of SAT or ACT scores is optional. [3]
Concentration: ['urban environmental studies', 'energy histories and geographies', 'environmental humanities']
Description: The transdisciplinary major in Environment, Geography, and Urbanization is housed in the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization (CEGU). The CEGU undergraduate major a prepares students to understand and confront the wide–ranging societal, historical, and spatial dimensions of contemporary planetary environmental crises, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and other forms of large–scale socio–environmental transformation. [2] Such issues are explored in diverse spaces, including cities and metropolitan regions; zones of extraction, agriculture, energy production, and waste; dispersed settlement spaces and village ecologies; rangeland, forest, and jungle landscapes; remote wildlands; and coastlines, rivers, watersheds, and oceans. [2] The curriculum emphasizes a plurality of theoretical approaches to the histories and geographies of socio–environmental transformation, underscoring the contested character of environmental knowledge in a polarized and turbulent world order. [2] The Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major consists of a sequence of foundational courses; substantive and methodological training in environmental, geographical, and urban studies; transdisciplinary electives spanning diverse thematic areas; and various capstone options, including the senior thesis and a community study. [2] The major provides students with strong foundations in spatialized and historical approaches to environmental studies, with more specialized thematic tracks available in several fields, including urban environmental studies, energy histories and geographies, and environmental humanities. [2] Through engagement with these fields of inquiry, students explore the wide–ranging social, historical, and spatial transformations that have produced the environmental emergencies of our time. [2] Graduates of the CEGU major will be well–equipped to conduct advanced research on socio–environmental processes, transformations, and crises across time and space, and to engage in diverse fields of urban and environmental practice. [2] The curriculum combines scholarly inquiry, methodological training, experiential learning, and community engagement to prepare students to contribute to—and transform—the collective process of forging more equitable, livable, and hopeful planetary futures. [2, 3]

ProgramName: Minor in Environment, Geography, and Urbanization
Requirements: Students who elect the minor program in Environment, Geography, and Urbanization (CEGU) should meet with the Student Affairs Administrator before the end of the Spring Quarter of their third year to declare their intention to complete the minor and select appropriate courses. [2] The approval of the program director for the minor program should be submitted to a student's College adviser on the Consent to Complete a Minor Program form. [3] A Minor Course of Study form must also be completed. [8]
Description: The minor program in Environment, Geography and Urbanization (CEGU) offers students the ability to explore a plurality of theoretical approaches to the histories and geographies of socio-environmental transformation through just six classes: three foundational courses in addition to three electives. [3] Similarly to the undergraduate major, the CEGU minor prepares students to understand and confront the wide-ranging societal, historical, and spatial dimensions of contemporary planetary environmental crises, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and other forms of large-scale socio-environmental transformation. [3]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Environmental and Urban Studies
Requirements: The University of Chicago uses a holistic application review process. While specific requirements for the phased-out Bachelor of Arts in Environmental and Urban Studies are not available, all undergraduate applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, a school report, high school transcript, and two teacher recommendations. The application includes essay questions.
Description: Students in Environmental and Urban Studies will gain an understanding of the interconnected natural and urban realms, developing fluency with ideas such as sustainable development, walkable urbanism, environmental justice, or political ecology, along with the opportunities and challenges they present. [1] The Environmental and Urban Studies major and minor programs are designed to motivate a deeper theoretical understanding of cities and nature as develop practical strength in addressing urban and environmental challenges. [1] Students begin the program through foundational courses focused on frameworks, theories and models of human-environment relationships, progress toward interdisciplinary methodological applications to topic-based experiential learning. The major program culminates in a BA Thesis or BA Capstone focused on addressing a critical urban environmental issue. [1] The Environmental and Urban Studies (ENST) major is only available to students who have already declared as of Spring 2023. [1] All new major declarations will be in Environment, Geography and Urbanization (CEGU). [1]

ProgramName: Minor in Environmental and Urban Studies
Department: Committee on Environment, Geography and Urbanization (CEGU), Division of Social Sciences

Description: Climate change, urban sprawl, habitat loss, pollution, food and energy needs, and their understanding as issues of social justice and economic stability are among the most pressing problems facing contemporary societies. [1] Environmental and urban patterns and processes operate at multiple scales involving natural and human causes and consequences that cannot be addressed within a single discipline. [1] Students in Environmental and Urban Studies will gain an understanding of the interconnected natural and urban realms, developing fluency with ideas such as sustainable development, walkable urbanism, environmental justice, or political ecology, along with the opportunities and challenges they present. [1] The Environmental and Urban Studies major and minor programs are designed to motivate a deeper theoretical understanding of cities and nature as develop practical strength in addressing urban and environmental challenges. [1] Students begin the program through foundational courses focused on frameworks, theories and models of human-environment relationships, progress toward interdisciplinary methodological applications to topic-based experiential learning. [1] The Environmental and Urban Studies (ENST) major is only available to students who have already declared as of Spring 2023. ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Gender and Sexuality Studies
Requirements: Prospective students apply to the University of Chicago's undergraduate College, not to a specific major. The university uses a holistic review process and requires the submission of the Common Application or Coalition Application, which includes personal essays and the UChicago Supplement with its own unique essay questions. Additionally, applicants must submit their high school transcripts and two teacher recommendations. While not explicitly stated as a requirement, a school report from a counselor is a standard part of the application.
Department: The College, Center for the Study of Gender and Sexuality
Fees: $71,325 per year for the 2025-2026 academic year. [4]
Description: The GNSE major is designed with flexibility in mind and is meant to provide students with the opportunity to design a course of study tailored to their particular interests. The major consists of 11 courses. Courses can be from a variety of disciplines, but all must be cross-listed with GNSE.
ScholarshipAmount: Merit-based scholarships start at $2,000. [18] The First Phoenix Scholarship provides $20,000 over four years. [18] Some scholarships offer full tuition. [19]

ProgramName: Minor in Gender and Sexuality Studies
Requirements: Choosing to pursue a minor allows you to shape a disciplinary or interdisciplinary plan of study that will provide a competence in gender and sexuality studies. Such a minor requires a total of six courses: GNSE 20001 or an approved substitute and five additional courses in Gender and Sexuality Studies. Students who elect the minor program in Gender and Sexuality Studies should meet with Bonnie Kanter, Assistant Director for Student Affairs and Curriculum (bonniek@uchicago.edu) before the end of Spring Quarter of their third year to declare their intention to complete the minor and discuss planned coursework. Approval for the minor program should be submitted to each student's College adviser by the deadline on a form obtained from the adviser. [2]
Description: Gender and Sexuality Studies at the University of Chicago encompasses diverse disciplines, modes of inquiry, and objects of knowledge. A minor in Gender and Sexuality Studies allows students in other major fields to shape a disciplinary or interdisciplinary plan of study that will provide a competence in gender and sexuality studies.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Geophysical Sciences
Requirements: Application requirements are not specific to the Bachelor of Arts in Geophysical Sciences but are for general undergraduate admission to The University of Chicago college. Prospective students apply to the university as a whole, not a specific major. General requirements include the Common Application or Coalition Application, responses to the UChicago Supplement essays, a secondary school report, official transcripts, and two teacher evaluations.
Department: The College, Department of the Geophysical Sciences
ScholarshipType: Need-based grants, merit-based scholarships, and various endowed scholarships.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Geophysical Sciences
Description: The Department of the Geophysical Sciences (GEOS) offers unique programs of study in the earth, atmospheric, and planetary sciences. Topics include the physics, chemistry, and dynamics of the atmosphere, oceans, and ice sheets; past and present climate change; the origin and history of the Earth, moon, and meteorites; properties of the deep interior of the Earth and the dynamics of crustal movements; and the evolution and geography of life and the Earth's surface environments through geologic time. These multidisciplinary topics require an integrated approach founded on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology. Both the BA and BS programs prepare students for careers that draw upon the earth, atmospheric, and planetary sciences. However, the BS degree provides a more focused and intensive program of study for students who intend to pursue graduate work in these disciplines.
ScholarshipAmount: Merit-based scholarships start at $2,000. [20] All first-generation students receive a minimum of $20,000 over four years. [16]
ScholarshipType: Merit-based, Need-based, First-generation, for dependents of faculty and staff, for students from the Chicagoland area, and for graduates of Chicago Public Schools.

Requirements: To declare the Minor in Germanic Studies, students must first complete the second-year language sequence or satisfy the prerequisite via examination. The minor requires three courses from the third-year sequence and three literature/culture courses, with specific rules about how many must be taught in German. Description: The Minor in Germanic Studies is designed for students who wish to reach advanced language proficiency in German and deepen their knowledge and understanding of German culture and literature. [5] Students minoring in Germanic Studies typically complete the second-year language sequence first, which is a prerequisite. [3] In addition, students typically register for three courses in the third-year sequence and three literature/culture courses, two of which must be taken in German. [3] Courses in the minor may not be double counted with the student's major(s) or with other minors and may not be counted toward general education requirements. [3, 5] Courses must be taken for quality grades, and more than half of the requirements must be met by registering for courses bearing University of Chicago course numbers. [3, 5]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Global Studies
Requirements: Applicants to The University of Chicago apply to the university as a whole, not to a specific major. The application requirements include the Common Application or Coalition Application, a school report, transcripts, two teacher recommendations, and the UChicago Supplement, which consists of a 'Why Us?' essay and an extended essay from a choice of prompts. [11, 15] While not explicitly called a statement of purpose, the UChicago Supplement essays serve a similar function in allowing applicants to express their interests and personality. [18] Students may also submit supplemental materials that highlight a significant talent or achievement, such as creative writing, research projects, or business plans. [18]
Description: Global Studies offers an integrated, interdisciplinary approach to an understanding of global issues. Our undergraduate major encourages a broad understanding of the world while exploring the diversity and richness of other cultures. Our program places particular emphasis on study abroad, independent research, and language coursework. [1]

ProgramName: Minor in Global Studies

ScholarshipType: Merit-based, Need-based, First-generation, and other specific scholarships are available. [5, 8]

ProgramName: Minor in Health and Society
Requirements: College students in any field of study may complete a minor in Health and Society. [2, 3] Students who wish to declare a minor in Health and Society must contact the program and fill out a minor map before the end of Spring Quarter of their third year to declare their intention to complete the minor. [3, 6] The minor requires a total of five courses, including one required introductory course (HLTH 17000, HLTH 17001, or HLTH 17050) and four approved elective courses. [2, 3]
Description: The Health and Society minor explores the social, political, and economic processes that shape individual and population health. [3] Disability, experiences of illness, categories of disorder, ideals of well-being, and models of medical intervention can all vary between cultural settings and across history. [3] Rapid changes in medicine and biotechnology create new understandings and expectations about illness, health, and well-being. [3] At the same time, inequalities in access to care and in health outcomes across populations, in the United States and globally, have become important to conversations in policy and practice alike. [3] To understand health in its broader contexts, this minor encompasses a range of disciplines and methods in the social sciences, and differential emphases on theory, practice, and policy implications. [3] A minor in Health and Society will provide a background for medical school, the allied health professions, public health, health policy, health advocacy, the study of law with an emphasis on health, and doctoral work in a range of social science disciplines. [3]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit awards start at $2,000 and can go up to full tuition.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in History
Requirements: Application requirements are for general undergraduate admission to The University of Chicago, not specifically for the History program. The supplement includes two required essays: one asking why you wish to attend UChicago, and another chosen from a list of creative prompts. ProgramName: Minor in History
Requirements: The history minor requires six total courses: Historiography (HIST 29803) and five HIST-numbered electives. [10, 13] Minor courses may not be double-counted with other majors or minors. [10] Students interested in officially declaring a minor should meet with the Director of Undergraduate Studies or other appointed department contact to discuss their interest and submit a completed Minor Consent Form to their Academic Adviser. [12] Any minors should be officially declared by the end of the student's third year. [12]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in History, Philosophy, and Social Studies of Science and Medicine
Concentration: ['History and Philosophy of Biological Science', 'Philosophy of Science', 'History of Medicine and Medical Ethics']
Description: The BA program in the History, Philosophy, and Social Studies of Science and Medicine (HIPS) Is an undergraduate program for students at the College interested in exploring the historical development, conceptual framework, and societal impact of science. [4] To establish a solid basis for analyzing the nature of science, students in the program are required to complete substantial coursework in one or more scientific disciplines. [4] After building this foundation, students are expected to develop an understanding of the origins of science and the evolution of scientific thought, influenced by both its internal dynamics and its interplay with the broader societal context in which it is situated. [4] The HIPS program is structured to facilitate the examination of a broad spectrum of social, historical, and conceptual topics related to science. [4] Graduates of the program pursue a variety of career paths. [4] Some continue their studies at the graduate level in the history and philosophy of science or a specific scientific field. [4] Others find the program provides valuable preparation for careers in medicine, law, public policy, or science journalism. [4] More broadly, the program aims to equip students with a strong foundation for interpreting and assessing science and science policy. [4]

ProgramName: Minor in History, Philosophy, and Social Studies of Science and Medicine
Description: Students in other fields of study may complete a minor in HIPS, in particular, the minor program in HIPS offers students who are majoring in science the opportunity to gain an understanding of the conceptual, historical, and social contexts in which their disciplines are situated. [2] The minor requires a total of six courses. [2] Courses in the minor (1) may not be double counted with the student's major(s) or with other minors and (2) may not be counted toward general education requirements. [2] The HIPS program is designed to make possible the study of a wide range of social, historical, and conceptual issues relating to science. [1] Students completing the program follow a number of different careers. [1] Some pursue graduate study in the history and philosophy of science or in some field of science. [1] Others find the program valuable preparation for the study of medicine, law, public policy, or science journalism. [1] More generally, the goal of the program is to provide students with a sound basis on which to interpret and evaluate science and science policy. [1]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Human Rights
Description: Our program provides a comprehensive education in the theory and practice of human rights, grounded in interdisciplinary study. Our curriculum draws on law, philosophy, history, and public policy to give you the rigorous knowledge and skills to critically understand real-world issues. You'll learn from renowned faculty members who are experts in their fields and gain hands-on experience through internships, research projects, and field trips. As a human rights major, you'll be well-prepared for a variety of career paths, including advocacy, policy-making, non-profit work, and more. [1]

ProgramName: Minor in Human Rights
Requirements: To declare a minor in Human Rights, students must receive approval from the Coordinator of Undergraduate Studies, Professor Ben Laurence.
