[7] The program requires the completion of five courses, which includes one introductory course and four approved Human Rights (HMRT) or cross-listed courses. [7]
Description: The human rights minor is an interdisciplinary program that provides students with a foundation in the theoretical, historical, and comparative perspectives on human rights. [2] The flexibility of this course of study complements any major. [2] A minor in human rights can provide a background for graduate study in many fields or for careers that incorporate human rights analysis or advocacy. [2] The minor requires a total of five courses, including one introductory course and four approved Human Rights (HMRT) courses or cross-listed courses. [2]

ProgramName: Minor in Inquiry and Research in the Humanities
Requirements: The University of Chicago uses a holistic application review process. While a complete, centralized list of all general application requirements is not available on the university's website, applicants are expected to submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, which includes a personal essay. The university has a test-optional policy, meaning applicants can choose whether or not to submit ACT or SAT scores. There are no general, institute-level requirements for a resume, statement of purpose, or writing sample for all undergraduate applicants; these may be requested by specific programs.
Description: The bachelor of arts degree program in Inquiry and Research in the Humanities (IRHUM) offers undergraduates the opportunity to pursue an individualized program of humanistic study in preparation of an independent, mentored research project, which will form the capstone experience of their College education at the University of Chicago. [2] IRHUM is thus not defined by a particular discipline or field, but by the techniques and practices of humanistic inquiry and research. [1, 2] For individual students pursuing the IRHUM major, cohesion is provided by the program of humanistic study, formal research training, and the final research project they design in consultation with the Faculty Chair and Co-Chair of IRHUM, and their disciplinarily focused faculty mentor(s). [2] Admission is by an application, in which students must clearly articulate their interest in humanistic research and describe the area of inquiry they plan to pursue. [1, 4] Centered in the humanities, the program of study may draw on subject areas, fields, and techniques from disciplines in the social, biological, and physical sciences. [1, 4]

ProgramName: Minor in Jewish Studies
Requirements: A minor in Jewish Studies is not listed as a standalone program in the University of Chicago's academic catalog. Jewish Studies falls under the Department of Middle Eastern Studies (formerly Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations). Students can pursue a minor in this department with a focus on relevant subjects. The general requirements for a minor in this department are six courses, with an option for a language or culture track. [2] Specific application requirements for a 'Minor in Jewish Studies' are not available on the University of Chicago website.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Latin American and Caribbean Studies
Requirements: Applicants can submit the Coalition Application or Common Application. The application includes a personal essay. In addition to the application, students must submit two teacher recommendations and their secondary school report and transcript. A mid-year report is also required. An application fee of $75 or a fee waiver is necessary. While not required, students may submit a 1-2 page document of any additional information they wish to convey to the admissions committee. Students may also submit an optional 2-minute video introduction.
Description: Latin American and Caribbean Studies (LACS) is an interdisciplinary program for students who want to engage critical issues in the social sciences and humanities through deep immersion in the histories, cultures, economies, politics, and natural environments of Latin America and the Caribbean. [2, 4, 5] In addition to gaining deep knowledge of a region closely tied to Chicago and the United States, LACS students will develop strong linguistic, research, and analytical skills; most also spend significant time studying or conducting fieldwork in a Latin American or Caribbean country. [4, 5] The major requirements include: coursework; language proficiency in Spanish or Portuguese; experiential learning that aims to broaden students' appreciation of Latin American and Caribbean perspectives and deepen their cultural fluency; and a fourth-year BA colloquium and capstone project that allow students to develop their capacity for independent, creative, rigorous inquiry. [4, 5]

ProgramName: Minor in Latin American and Caribbean Studies
Requirements: To declare the minor in Latin American and Caribbean Studies, students should meet with the LACS program adviser to go over their plan of study. The minor must be declared online via my.uchicago no later than the Spring Quarter of the student's third year. [2] The program is designed for students already majoring in other disciplines at the university. [2] The requirements for completing the minor include coursework, language proficiency in Spanish or Portuguese, and the submission of a research paper from a LACS course. [2, 3]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Law, Letters, and Society
Requirements: Applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, a non-refundable application fee or fee waiver, a Secondary School Report and transcript, two teacher recommendations, and a mid-year report. The application includes a personal essay and two university-specific supplemental essays.
Department: The College, Social Sciences Collegiate Division

ProgramName: Minor in Law, Letters, and Society
Bachelor of Arts in Linguistics
Requirements: First-year applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, the UChicago Supplement essays, a high school transcript, and two teacher recommendations. An optional video profile and/or a portfolio for select programs may also be submitted.
Description: Linguistics is the scientific study of language. The undergraduate program in linguistics at the University of Chicago is designed to provide students with a solid foundation in the core areas of the field — phonology, syntax, and semantics/pragmatics — and to provide opportunities for further study in these and other areas of linguistics and related disciplines. The program is structured to give students a strong background for graduate study, and also to be a valuable component of a liberal arts education for students who do not intend to continue in linguistics. Students can pursue a 10-course minor, a 12-course major, or a 14-course intensive major. The intensive major is recommended for students who are considering graduate study in linguistics. The program also participates in a joint BA/MA program.

ProgramName: Minor in Linguistics
Department: The College, Division of the Humanities
Description: Students who are majoring in other fields of study may also complete a minor in linguistics. To do so, they must complete a total of six courses in linguistics, of which two must be LING 20101 Introduction to Phonetics and Phonology, LING 20201 Introduction to Syntax, or LING 20301 Introduction to Semantics and Pragmatics. At least four of the six courses must be courses in the Department of Linguistics (LING). All courses for the minor must be taken for quality grades.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Mathematics
Requirements: Application requirements for first-year applicants include the Common Application or Coalition Application, the UChicago Supplement (which consists of two essays), a secondary school report and transcript, and two teacher recommendations.
Description: All undergraduate degrees in the department are based ɔn α four-course sequence in calculus and differential equations and have α computational component. The mathematics and applied mathematics degrees all require further mathematics courses in analysis and algebra. The statistics degrees all require α further statistics core. The applied mathematics program has α four-course professional core requirement to promote the understanding of how mathematics is applied in other fields. There are additional requirements particular to each degree program, including technical electives in the major.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Mathematics
Requirements: The University of Chicago uses a holistic application review process. Applicants can apply using the Common Application or the Coalition Application and must submit required supplementary materials, which include the UChicago Supplement. The supplement consists of a "Why Us?" essay and an extended essay from a choice of prompts. Other requirements include a high school transcript, a school report, and two teacher recommendations. The university does not have a minimum GPA requirement, as academic and extracurricular achievements are considered in the context of the applicant's background and opportunities.
Concentration: BS in Mathematics with Specialization in Economics
Description: Four bachelor's degrees are available in the Department of Mathematics: the BA in mathematics, the BS in mathematics, the BS in applied mathematics, and the BS in mathematics with specialization in economics. The Department of Mathematics provides an environment of research and comprehensive instruction in mathematics and applied mathematics at both undergraduate and graduate levels. [2, 15] At the undergraduate level, we offer four degrees: a Bachelor of Arts (BA) in Mathematics, a Bachelor of Science (BS) in Mathematics, a Bachelor of Science in Applied Mathematics, and a Bachelor of Science in Mathematics with Specialization in Economics. [2]
Accredidation: Since 1913, the University of Chicago has been continuously accredited by the Higher Learning Commission. [13]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Mathematics with a Specialization in Applied Mathematics
Bachelor of Science in Mathematics with a Specialization in Computer Science
Requirements: The University of Chicago accepts the Common Application and the Coalition Application. Applicants must also submit the UChicago Supplement, which includes a "Why UChicago?" essay and an extended essay. Additional required documents include a high school transcript, a school report, two teacher recommendations, and a counselor recommendation. An application fee is required, though waivers are available. [2, 12, 13, 21]
Description: The concentration program leading to a B.S. in mathematics with a specialization in computer science is a version of the B.S. in mathematics. The degree will be in mathematics with the designation "with specialization in computer science" included on the final transcript. [6]

ProgramName: Minor in Mathematics
Requirements: To be admitted to the minor, students must have successfully completed a semester of linear algebra (MATH 2210, 2230, or 2940) with a grade of B– or better, and a semester of multivariable calculus (MATH 2220, 2240, or 1920) with a grade of B– or better. The minor requires the completion of four 3000- or 4000-level MATH courses, with at least one at the 4000 level or above. At least one course must be in algebra and one in analysis. Courses must be taken for a letter grade, with a grade of C– or better received. [1]
Description: Students in other fields of study may also complete a minor in mathematics; information for the minor follows the description of the major. [4]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Media Arts and Design
Requirements: Applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. The application includes two required supplemental essays: a 'Why UChicago?' essay and an extended essay from a choice of prompts. Additionally, applicants must provide teacher recommendations and a school report. [2, 3, 5]
Department: Division of the Humanities, Department of Cinema and Media Studies
ScholarshipAmount: The 'No Barriers' program offers free tuition for families with incomes under $125,000 per year. [4]
ScholarshipPercentage: 49% of undergraduate students receive financial aid. [16]

ProgramName: Minor in Medieval Studies
Requirements: Students must complete the Consent to Complete a Minor Program form, which requires the signature of the director of the undergraduate program in medieval studies. Students must submit a copy of the signed approval form to their College adviser by the deadline on the form. [7]
Description: The undergraduate Program in Medieval Studies offers an interdisciplinary major and minor, which allow students to explore the history, literature, art, philosophy, theology and cultural production of the Middle Ages in an integrated and nuanced fashion, through engagement with a diverse array of textual and material artifacts. [9]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Molecular Engineering
Requirements: To apply for the Bachelor of Science in Molecular Engineering, prospective students must apply for general admission to The College of the University of Chicago. The application requires a high school transcript, letters of recommendation, and application essays, including the UChicago Supplement with its well-known "Uncommon Essay" prompts. [16] There is no separate application to declare the molecular engineering major. [5]
Description: The BS degree in Molecular Engineering offers undergraduates a cutting-edge engineering curriculum built on a strong foundation in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology. [2] Courses in the major are designed to develop quantitative reasoning and problem-solving skills; to introduce engineering analysis of biological, chemical, and physical systems; and to address open-ended technological questions across a spectrum of disciplines. [2] The aim is to introduce invention and design, along with inquiry and discovery, as fruitful and complementary intellectual activities. [2] The program prepares undergraduates for leadership roles in a technology-driven society. Graduates will be positioned to follow traditional engineering paths in research, technology development, and manufacturing, or to pursue further postgraduate study in such fields as engineering, science, medicine, business, or law. [2] Other graduates may successfully leverage the quantitative and problem-solving skills gained in their training as engineers towards careers in technical and management consulting, finance, public policy, or entrepreneurship. [2]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Molecular Engineering with an Area of Study in Biology
Description: The BS degree in Molecular Engineering offers undergraduates acutting-edge engineering curriculum built on a strong foundation in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology. Courses in the major are designed to develop quantitative reasoning and problem-solving skills; to introduce engineering analysis of biological, chemical, and physical systems; and to address open-ended technological questions across a spectrum of disciplines. The aim is to introduce invention and design, along with inquiry and discovery, as fruitful and complementary intellectual activities. [1] The Molecular Engineering program allows students to select one of three tracks—bioengineering, chemical engineering, or quantum engineering—to concentrate and deepen knowledge in the area that interests them the most. [1] The Bioengineering Track includes a bioengineering laboratory and courses in organic chemistry, biochemistry, quantitative physiology, systems biology, and cellular engineering. [1]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Molecular Engineering with an Area of Study in Chemical and Soft Materials
Requirements: Application requirements for all undergraduate programs at The University of Chicago are handled centrally through the admissions office. Applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. This includes the applicant's responses to the UChicago Supplement questions and essays, an official secondary school transcript, and two teacher recommendations. Application materials are the same for all students, regardless of their intended major.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Molecular Engineering with an Area of Study in Quantum
Requirements: Applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, which includes a personal essay. The University of Chicago also requires a supplement with two additional essays: one on why you wish to attend the university and another chosen from a list of prompts. [3, 14] Other requirements include a high school transcript, a school report, and two teacher recommendations. [3]
Department: Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering and The College

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Music
Requirements: To apply for the Bachelor of Arts in Music, prospective students must submit a first-year application through the Common Application or Coalition Application. The University of Chicago also requires the UChicago Supplement, which includes an optional two-minute video introduction and specific essay questions. While there are no specific high school course requirements, students are encouraged to pursue a challenging curriculum. For those interested in the music program, an optional Arts Supplement can be submitted to showcase musical talents. Standardized test scores (ACT/SAT) are optional for applicants through the 2025-2026 application cycle. Additionally, two teacher recommendations are required.
Fees: The undergraduate tuition for the 2025-2026 academic year is $71,325. [9] There is no specific tuition fee mentioned for the Bachelor of Arts in Music program.
Description: The music major requires 1100 units of study. Six "foundation" courses are chosen from the following areas: Analysis and Techniques, Histories and Cultures, and Creative Practices. Majors are required to earn at least 1100 units of music course work divided between analytical, historical, cultural, and creative practices. Students have considerable agency to design a major that accords with their own interests, with an additional option to write a BA thesis or composition eligible for special honors. Students plan and formalize their major program of study in consultation with the Director of Undergraduate Studies. The Music Major presents a balanced selection of courses in music history, performance, theory, and literature. It prepares Music Majors for graduate and professional training in the art of music, but the Major also appeals to students planning careers in various fields.
ScholarshipAmount: Merit-based awards start at $2,000. The First Phoenix Scholarship provides $20,000 over four years. [7]
ScholarshipType: Need-Based Aid and Merit-Based Scholarships. [23] Specific scholarships include the Odyssey Scholarship, First Phoenix Scholarship, and various scholarships for students from the Chicago area. [7, 14]

ProgramName: Minor in Music
Requirements: To declare a Minor in Music, a current student must meet with the Director of Undergraduate Studies before the end of the spring quarter of their third year to declare their intention and submit a completed and signed Minor Consent Form to their Academic Adviser. [5, 9] The program requires the completion of seven courses, including four in the Foundations of music and three Electives, as well as participation for at least three quarters in a performance organization approved by the Department of Music. [4, 5]
Description: The minor in music requires students to engage with musical theories, materials, and techniques, the study of music in history and culture, and performance. At the same time, it provides students with the flexibility to emphasize areas that interest them most. Those enrolled in the music minor are considered members of the Department of Music and are encouraged to participate in all program activities. [2]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations
Requirements: Application requirements for all undergraduate programs at The University of Chicago include the Coalition Application or Common Application, a supplemental essay specific to UChicago, two teacher recommendations, and a secondary school report with an official transcript. Submission of SAT or ACT scores is optional.
Department: The College, Division of the Humanities
Concentration: ['Arabic Studies', 'Armenian Studies', 'Archaeology and Art of the Ancient Near East', 'Classical Hebrew Language and Civilization', 'Cuneiform Studies', 'Egyptian Languages and Civilization', 'History', 'Islamic Thought', 'Israeli and Jewish Studies', 'Persian and Iranian Studies', 'Semitic Languages and Literatures', 'Turkish and Ottoman Studies']
Description: Loosely defined as stretching from Morocco in the west to Iran and Afghanistan in the east, the region is home some of the world's great religions and civilizations. Historically, the influence of its languages, literatures and cultures has extended to Central, East and Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, Europe and North America. Thus, the study of the Near and Middle East is an important academic area of ​​academic study on account of its political, economic and cultural significance on the international stage. The concentration offers students a multi-faceted and inter-disciplinary perspective on Near Middle Eastern cultures and languages ​​that have been so influential throughout the world. Undergraduate concentrators develop skills in one or more of the languages ​​of the region on their way to choosing from a wide variety of directions of study. The Department offers instruction in a range of ancient and modern languages ​​including Akkadian, Arabic, Aramaic, Armenian, Egyptian, Hebrew, Iranian, Persian, Sumerian, Turkish (Ottoman and Modern), and Yiddish. The concentration provides a solid grounding in the student's area of ​​focus and offers an in-depth look at how scholars explore these languages ​​and their associated cultures that have been so influential throughout the world. Undergraduate students have the option of applying for an AB/AM degree. The NELC concentration will be of interest to students who are considering careers in academia, government and Foreign Service, law, journalism, education, business, and divinity, among others, as well as those who anticipate graduate study in Near Eastern or related fields. One of the strengths of the concentration in Near Eastern Languages ​​and Civilizations is the individual attention each student receives in pursuing his or her interests within the broader arena of the Near/Middle Eastern Studies.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Arabic Studies
Concentration: Islamic and Modern Middle Eastern Studies (including Arabic, Armenian, Modern Hebrew, Kazakh, Persian, Turkish, and Uzbek)
Description: The BA degree programs in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations (NELC) are as varied as the wide subject matter they embrace. Areas of specialization within NELC include: Archaeology and Art of the Ancient Near East; Classical Hebrew Language and Civilization; Cuneiform Studies (including Assyriology, Hittitology, and Sumerology); Egyptology/Egyptian Languages and Civilization; Islamic and Modern Middle Eastern Studies (including Arabic, Armenian, Modern Hebrew, Kazakh, Persian, Turkish, and Uzbek); Near Eastern Judaica. Students who major in NELC learn one or more of the primary native languages as a means of access to the cultures of the ancient Near East and the modern Middle East. Students who plan to do advanced work in Near Eastern studies are strongly encouraged also to develop a reading knowledge of German and French. In consultation with the counselor for undergraduate studies, each student chooses an area of specialization and devises a program of study that provides a sound basis for graduate work in that area or for a career in museology, business, government, or other disciplines. [1]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Armenian Studies
Requirements: To apply for undergraduate admission to The University of Chicago, applicants can use the Common Application or Coalition Application. The university has a holistic review process and considers a candidate's entire application, including academic records, extracurriculars, essays, and letters of recommendation. [2] The application requires a Common App essay and UChicago-specific supplemental essays, often referred to as the "Uncommon Essay," which are designed to showcase an applicant's creativity and intellectual curiosity. [7] Recommendations are also required. [11] While not explicitly required, applicants can create a list of their extracurricular activities and achievements to include on their application or as a résumé. [15] The university also offers an optional two-minute video introduction for all students. [8]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Archaeology and Art of the Ancient Near East
Requirements: Applicants to the University of Chicago undergraduate college are required to submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. The application includes several components: supplemental essays (including the well-known "Uncommon Essay"), two teacher recommendations, a secondary school report and transcript, and an application fee or a fee waiver. [6, 11] Mid-year reports are also required. [13]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Classical Hebrew Language and Civilization

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Cuneiform Studies
Requirements: Prospective students apply to the University of Chicago through the Common Application or the Coalition Application. The application includes personal essays, and applicants have the option to submit a two-minute video introduction. Recommendations are required from two teachers and a secondary school counselor. Official high school transcripts are also necessary. The university has a test-optional policy for SAT and ACT scores.
Description: The BA degree programs in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations (NELC) are as varied as the wide subject matter they embrace. Areas of specialization within NELC include: Archaeology and Art of the Ancient Near East; Classical Hebrew Language and Civilization; Cuneiform Studies (including Assyriology, Hittitology, and Sumerology); Egyptology/Egyptian Languages and Civilization; Islamic and Modern Middle Eastern Studies; and Near Eastern Judaica. All three subfields require an advanced knowledge of the major language, and the relevant history and archaeology. [1]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Egyptian Languages and Civilization
Requirements: To apply as a first-year student to the University of Chicago, applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. This includes the main essay from either platform, as well as the UChicago Supplement, which consists of specific essay questions. Other required materials include a secondary school report with an official transcript, a school counselor recommendation, and two teacher recommendations.
Description: The BA degree programs in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations (NELC) are as varied as the wide subject matter they embrace. Areas of specialization within NELC include: Archaeology and Art of the Ancient Near East; Classical Hebrew Language and Civilization; Cuneiform Studies (including Assyriology, Hittitology, and Sumerology); Egyptology/Egyptian Languages and Civilization; Islamic and Modern Middle Eastern Studies (including Arabic, Armenian, Modern Hebrew, Kazakh, Persian, Turkish, and Uzbek); Near Eastern Judaica. ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in History
Requirements: Applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, along with the UChicago Supplement, which includes a 'Why Us?' essay and an extended essay from a selection of unique prompts. Additionally, two teacher recommendations and a secondary school report with a counselor recommendation and an official high school transcript are required.
Concentration: While the university offers various areas of specialization within Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, a specific track named 'Specialization in History' for the Bachelor of Arts is not explicitly detailed as a formal concentration on the main program pages. [1] Students do, however, devise a program of study in consultation with an advisor which can include a focus on history. [1]
Description: The Bachelor of Arts degree programs in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations (NELC) are designed to be as varied as the subject matter they cover. Students learn one or more primary native languages to access the cultures of the ancient Near East and the modern Middle East. In consultation with a counselor, each student selects an area of specialization and creates a program of study. This program is intended to build a strong foundation for graduate work in that area or for careers in fields such as museology, business, or government. The program encourages students who plan to pursue advanced studies to also develop a reading knowledge of German and French. [1]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Islamic Thought
Requirements: The University of Chicago uses the Common Application and the Coalition Application. General application components for undergraduate admission include the application form, supplemental essays (including the "Uncommon Essay"), a secondary school report and official transcript, and two teacher recommendations as well as one from a counselor. For graduate admissions, application requirements are determined by each individual school and program. [6, 8, 11]
Description: The Middle Eastern Studies major allows students to gain expertise in a wide variety of languages and learn critical evaluation methods from archaeologists, economists, historians, linguists, and literary scholars. The program focuses on the region from the Nile to the Oxus and Danube to the Indus, covering prehistory to the present day. [2] A specific course sequence, Islamic Thought and Literature I-II-III, explores the thought and literature of the Islamic world from the seventh century C.E. to the modern era. [2] This sequence covers key aspects of Islamic intellectual history, including scripture, law, theology, philosophy, literature, mysticism, political thought, historical writing, and archaeology. [2]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Israeli and Jewish Studies
Requirements: Application to the Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Israeli and Jewish Studies is handled through the general undergraduate admissions process for The College at the University of Chicago. There are no separate application requirements for this specific major. General requirements include the Common Application or Coalition Application, the UChicago Supplement which includes the extended essay (the "Uncommon Essay") and a shorter essay, a secondary school report and transcript, and two teacher recommendations.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Persian and Iranian Studies
Concentration: Islamic and Modern Middle Eastern Studies (including Arabic, Armenian, Modern Hebrew, Kazakh, Persian, Turkish, and Uzbek)

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Semitic Languages and Literatures
Requirements: General application requirements for undergraduate admission at The University of Chicago apply. The application includes a form, high school transcript, GPA, letters of recommendation, and application essays. [5, 10] Applicants are expected to have a strong high school academic record with coursework in English, mathematics, social sciences, and laboratory science. [3] A key part of the application is the 'Uncommon Essay,' which features creative and open-ended prompts designed to showcase an applicant's individuality and intellectual curiosity. [3]
ScholarshipType: Merit-based, need-based, academic, athletic, community service, minority, first-generation, military, and identity-based awards. [32]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations with a Specialization in Turkish and Ottoman Studies
Requirements: Applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application. All applicants must also submit the UChicago Supplement, which includes two required essays: a 'Why UChicago?' essay and an extended essay chosen from a list of creative prompts.
Description: The major in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations (NELC) explores the history and cultural traditions of the ancient, classical, and modern Middle East, including northeast Africa. Students acquire proficiency in languages and skills for interpreting literature, art, and material culture from ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia; late antiquity and Classical Islam; or the contemporary moment, explored through the modern languages of Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, and Turkish. [10] Specializations are available in: Arabic Studies; Armenian Studies; Archaeology and Art of the Ancient Near East; Classical Hebrew Language and Civilization; Cuneiform Studies; Egyptian Languages and Civilization; History; Islamic Thought; Israeli and Jewish Studies; Persian and Iranian Studies; Semitic Languages and Literatures; Turkish and Ottoman Studies. [6]

ProgramName: Minor in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations
Requirements: The minor in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations requires a total of six courses. Students may choose one of two tracks: (1) a language track that includes three courses of one NELC language at any level, or (2) a culture track that replaces language study with courses in such topics as archaeology, history, religion, or literature in translation. [2, 7] Both tracks require a two- or three-quarter NELC civilization sequence. [2, 7] Students who wish to take a minor in NELC must meet with the counselor for undergraduate studies before the end of Spring Quarter of their third year to declare their intention to complete the minor. [2, 7] Courses must be chosen in consultation with the counselor. [7] Students must submit the counselor's approval for the minor program to their College adviser by the specified deadline on a form obtained from the adviser. [7]
Concentration: Students may choose one of two tracks: (1) a language track that includes three courses of one NELC language at any level, or (2) a culture track that replaces language study with courses in such topics as archaeology, history, religion, or literature in translation. [1]
Description: The minor in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations (NELC) is for students who major in other fields. The minor requires a total of six courses. Students can choose between a language track, which includes three courses in one NELC language, or a culture track, which focuses on subjects like archaeology, history, religion, or literature. [1, 2] Both options require a two- or three-quarter NELC civilization sequence. [1] Students interested in the minor must declare their intention with the counselor for undergraduate studies before the end of the Spring Quarter of their third year. [1]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit-based awards start at $2,000; some scholarships cover full tuition, and the First Phoenix Scholarship provides $20,000 over four years. [3]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Neuroscience
Requirements: All first-year applicants must submit either the Coalition Application or the Common Application. In addition to the application form, students must submit a high school transcript, two teacher recommendations, and the UChicago Supplement, which includes a 'Why UChicago?' essay and an extended essay from a choice of creative prompts. The university has a test-optional policy, allowing students to choose whether or not to submit ACT or SAT scores. Submission of a portfolio or research is an option for students who have a special talent in a particular area.
Description: Neuroscience is the multidisciplinary study of nervous systems. The sheer scope of neuroscience necessitates numerous scientific approaches to achieve an understanding of sensation, perception, cognition, and behavior. Consequently, students in the major are provided with access to a wealth of scientific variety including biology, psychology, physics, chemistry, computer science, engineering, mathematics, statistics, and medicine. Neuroscience faculty at the University of Chicago have expertise in all of these areas and are distributed across the Biological Sciences, Social Sciences, and Physical Sciences Divisions. The course of study in the undergraduate major in neuroscience (NSCI) provides students with the background and skills appropriate to pursue a diverse set of careers. These include established neuroscience career paths in academia, medicine, and the pharmaceutical industry as well as new emerging careers in economics, machine learning, and analytics, to name but a few.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Neuroscience
Requirements: Applicants can use the Common Application or the Coalition Application. [14] Required materials include the UChicago Supplement, which consists of a 'Why UChicago?' essay and an extended essay from a choice of prompts (known as the 'Uncommon Essay'), as well as two teacher recommendations and a secondary school report. [8, 14] A strong high school academic record with coursework in English, mathematics, laboratory sciences, and social sciences is also expected. [15]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit awards start at $2,000. The First Phoenix Scholarship provides $20,000 over four years.
ScholarshipType: Merit-based, need-based, UChicago College Scholarship for Dependents of Faculty, Other Academic Appointees & Staff, First Phoenix Scholarship, Chicago Public Schools Scholarship, City Colleges of Chicago (CCC) Star Scholarship.

ProgramName: Minor in Norwegian Studies
Description: Students in any discipline may complete a minor in Norwegian Studies. [3] The program consists of the beginning language sequence (NORW 10100-10200-10300 First-Year Norwegian I-II-III) and three additional elective courses chosen in consultation with the program administrator. [3] Elective options include intermediate-level courses like NORW 10400 Intermediate Norwegian I: Introduction to Literature and NORW 10500 Intermediate Norwegian II, or any 20000-level Norwegian language and/or literature courses. [3] The language courses aim to provide students with proficiency in speaking, reading, writing, and listening, with a particular emphasis on speaking. [6] To declare the minor, students must meet with the program administrator before the end of the Spring Quarter of their third year. [6] Courses for the minor cannot be double-counted with a major or another minor and must be taken for quality grades. [6]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit awards range by amount, starting at $2,000. [14]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Philosophy
Concentration: ['The Intensive Major', 'The Major in Philosophy and Allied Fields']
Description: The undergraduate program in Philosophy trains students to think clearly and critically about the deepest and broadest questions concerning being, knowledge, and value, as well as their connections to the full range of human activities and interests. [2] The Philosophy major presents students with the perspectives of past thinkers and introduces them to a variety of methods of reasoning and judgment formation. [2] Courses in the major equip students with core skills involved in critical reading, analytical thinking, sound argumentation, and the clear, well-organized expression of ideas. [2] The department offers a curriculum that allows undergraduates to engage with all facets of the subject, including its humanistic, technical, historical, and contemporary dimensions. [9] Philosophy has both a theoretical aspect (epistemology, metaphysics, philosophy of language, philosophy of science) and a practical one (ethics, political philosophy, philosophy of law). [9] The University of Chicago offers a standard major, an intensive track for qualified students interested in small group discussions, and an option in philosophy and allied fields for interdisciplinary study. [14]

ProgramName: Minor in Philosophy
Description: A minor program is offered in Philosophy. This program is intended to provide a basic introduction to some of the central figures and themes in the history of philosophy and to some of the most challenging contemporary work. Students in the College who are interested in the formal declaration of a Minor in Philosophy should contact the Director of Undergraduate Studies. All students are required to meet with the Director of Undergraduate Studies or the Assistant to the Director of Undergraduate Studies at the time of declaration to have their course plan approved. The minor is not open to students who are majoring in Philosophy.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Physics
Bachelor of Science in Physics
Minor in Physics
Description: Physics is concerned with the study of space and time, matter and energy, forces and fields, and the fundamental laws that relate them to the universe. The undergraduate curriculum in the Department of Physics covers the broad fundamentals necessary for further study in theoretical or experimental physics, as well as allied fields in science and engineering. The physics major offers both BA and BS degrees. Students who are majoring in other fields of study may also complete a minor in physics. [2] The minor in physics offers a slate of courses that provides a firm grounding in the basics with sufficient flexibility to accommodate the needs and interests of those likely to pursue this line of study. [7]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Political Science
Minor in Political Science
Bachelor of Arts in Psychology
Description: The psychology major introduces students to the fundamentals of scientific psychology, providing a firm basis of psychological knowledge and research experience. The requirements of the major are designed to acquaint students with the research methods psychologists use and to provide a foundation of core knowledge covering the major areas of psychology. This broad foundation allows students to pursue a more advanced understanding of subfields related to their own particular interests and goals for the major. The program may serve as preparation for graduate work in psychology or related fields (e.g., neuroscience, education), as well as for students interested in careers in social work, public policy, business, or medicine.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Public Policy Studies
Concentration: ['Urban Policy', 'Data Science', 'Human Rights', 'Education Policy', 'Health Policy', 'International Development', 'Environmental Policy']
Description: Public Policy Studies is a multidisciplinary major grounded in the social sciences, with substantial inputs from economics, sociology, political science, and law, among other disciplines. The major recognizes that public issues are not neatly contained within traditional disciplinary boundaries and that analysts possessing a broad range of social scientific understanding, quantitative expertise, and communication skills are well placed to contribute to improved public policies. The program of study for the BA degree in public policy studies is designed to introduce students to policy analysis and implementation, equip them to use quantitative and economic techniques and methods, train them in policy research, and give them a thorough grounding in one or more specific policy areas.
ScholarshipAmount: Merit awards range by amount, starting at $2,000.

ProgramName: Minor in Public Policy Studies
Minor in Quantitative Social Analysis
Description: Die Nebenfachrichtung Quantitative Sozialanalyse befasst sich mit Statistik und Mathematik, um das Verhalten und die Erfahrungen von Einzelpersonen, Gruppen und Organisationen zu verstehen. [2] Es entwickelt starke statistische Grundlagen, um zu lernen, wie man gültige Schlussfolgerungen aus quantifizierbaren Daten zieht und empirische Belege in den Sozial-, Verhaltens- und Gesundheitswissenschaften kritisch bewertet. [2] Ein Nebenfach in quantitativer Sozialanalyse bietet eine hervorragende Grundlage für die Bewerbung für ein weiterführendes Studium auf verschiedenen Niveaus und in vielen Disziplinen. [2] Sein interdisziplinärer Charakter bietet den Studierenden eine breite Wissensbasis in den Sozialwissenschaften, der öffentlichen Ordnung und dem öffentlichen Gesundheitswesen und bietet eine einzigartige Perspektive, die in traditionellen Abteilungsprogrammen normalerweise nicht zu finden ist. [2, 7]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Religious Studies
Description:
The undergraduate program in Religious Studies is administered by the Divinity School. It offers a major and a minor in Religious Studies to students in the College.

Religious claims and institutions affect our cultural and political lives, global affairs, and personal formation, for good and for ill. Students of religion study the historical development of specific religious traditions, understand and critically engage the ethical and intellectual teachings of various religions, and begin to make some comparative appraisals of the roles that religions play in different cultures and historical periods. Religious beliefs and practices have shaped and continue to shape individuals' and groups' perception of themselves and the world around them. Religion touches all facets of human experience, and the Religious Studies program is the place to investigate its intersection with other spheres like gender and sexuality, race, the nation-state, violence, memory, ethics, emotions, politics, economy, power, art, literature, and media.

ProgramName: Minor in Religious Studies
Description: The minor in Religious Studies requires a total of six courses. RLST 10100 Introduction to Religious Studies is not required of minors, but it is strongly recommended that minors complete this foundational course. Courses should be chosen to reflect a broad understanding of the academic study of religion. Students must take at least one course in two of our three areas of study [Historical Studies (A), Constructive Studies (B), and Cultural Studies (C)]. Students in the program are able to explore numerous religious traditions, including Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, and Judaism, and are exposed to the sources, problems, methods, and methodologies of our diverse areas of study, including Biblical and Historical Studies; Ethics, Theology, and the Philosophy of Religions; as well as History of Religions, Anthropology, Sociology, and Religion and Literature. Religion touches all facets of human experience, and the religious studies program is the place to investigate its intersection with other spheres like gender and sexuality, race, the nation-state, violence, memory, ethics, emotions, politics, economy, power, art, literature, and media. [2, 3, 6]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Romance Languages and Literatures
Description: The Department of Romance Languages and Literatures (RLLT) offers several programs of study leading to the BA degree in French, Italian, or Spanish literature and culture; or in some combination, which may include Catalan, Portuguese, Basque, Haitian Creole (Kreyòl), or non-Romance languages of the Iberian Peninsula, the Caribbean, and Latin America. The BA programs are designed to give students knowledge of the literature and culture of their area of concentration, as well as to develop their linguistic competence in one or more of the Romance languages. Students in other fields of study may also complete a minor in RLLT. [13]

ProgramName: Minor in Romance Languages and Literatures
Concentration: Minor Program in Romance Languages, Literatures, and Cultures (Multiple Languages)
Description: This minor is designed to accommodate the needs and interests of students who would like to broaden their linguistic, literary, and cultural experience beyond the scope of monolingual programs. Romance languages have never existed in isolation and, now more than ever, we live in a globalized society that traverses linguistic borders. This minor prepares students to flourish in an increasingly multicultural and multilingual world.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Russian and East European Studies
Description: The Slavic Department's Russian and East European Studies (REES) BA degree program is designed to provide students with skills and facility in the languages and cultures of the region. [9] The BA in REES requires twelve (12) courses, which fall into four categories: courses in the major language of study, a Gateway course, a REES Proseminar and elective courses. [9] In this way students have the flexibility to construct a course of study that accords with their interests. [9] Our program prepares students for graduate work as well as for careers in government, NGOs, human rights, law, international business, translation, teaching, and research. [12]

ProgramName: Minor in Russian and East European Studies
Department: Center for East European and Russian/Eurasian Studies (CEERES) / Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures
Description: The Minor in Russian and East European Studies requires seven courses, including at least three language courses at the 20000 level or beyond. The first-year level of the major language of study cannot be counted toward the minor. The minor also requires at least two REES subject courses, one of which must be a Gateway-Designated Course. For the minor in REES, electives may include any level of another REES language beyond the major language of study. [10]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit-based scholarships start at $2,000. The First Phoenix Scholarship provides $20,000 over four years.

ProgramName: Minor in Sanskrit
Requirements: The process to declare a minor in South Asian Languages and Civilizations (which includes Sanskrit) is for currently enrolled students. Students must receive the approval of the SALC Director of Undergraduate Studies on a 'Minor Consent Form' obtained from their College adviser and return it by the Spring Quarter of their third year. Students must also indicate their intent to minor in SALC with a form obtained from the SALC Director of Undergraduate Studies. [9] The academic requirements for the minor involve completing six or seven courses from specific categories. [8, 9]
Department: Department of South Asian Languages and Civilizations
Description: The minor program in South Asian Languages and Civilizations requires a total of six or seven courses, depending on whether the sequence SALC 20100-20200 Introduction to the Civilizations of South Asia I-II or two quarters of the SOSC 23004-23005 South Asian Civilizations in India I-II sequence taught in Pune are used to meet the general education requirement or to meet the minor program. [1] All students in the minor are required to take two quarters of SALC 20100-20200 Introduction to the Civilizations of South Asia I-II or SOSC 19016-19017-19018 South Asian Civilizations in India I-II-III (taught in Pune). [2] If these are not used to meet the general education requirement, both courses must be included in the minor, for a total of seven courses. [2] The minor also requires a two-quarter sequence of a South Asian language at the second-year level or above, and two additional courses that may be SALC courses, language courses, or courses on South Asia from other departments with approval. [2]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit-based scholarships start at $2,000 and can go up to full tuition.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Slavic Languages and Literatures
Requirements: Applicants to the Bachelor of Arts in Slavic Languages and Literatures follow the general application requirements for first-year applicants to The University of Chicago. These include the submission of the Coalition Application or Common Application, a supplemental essay as part of the application, a secondary school report and transcript, and two teacher recommendations. There is no specific application or set of requirements for this major at the undergraduate level.
Concentration: ['Russian Language and Literature or Russian Linguistics', 'West Slavic (Czech or Polish) Languages and Literatures', 'Interdisciplinary Studies in Balkan, Baltic, and Slavic']
Description: The Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures offers courses in the Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian, Czech, Polish, and Russian languages and literatures, and in Slavic linguistics and other general Slavic and East European subjects. The department also offers a program leading to the BA degree in Slavic Languages and Literatures. Students choose one of three areas of concentration to meet the requirements of this major. [2] The Slavic Department's Russian and East European Studies (REES) BA program provides students with language mastery, cultural competence, and critical thinking —skills essential for responding to the complexities of today's global world. The program prepares students for graduate work as well as for careers in government, NGOs, human rights, law, international business, translation, teaching, and research. [3] The department offers a wide range of interdisciplinary courses in Russian and East European literature, film, history and culture, as well as excellent language training in Russian, Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian, Polish, Czech, and Ukrainian. The program provides customized courses of study, which students design in conjunction with faculty members. [12]

ProgramName: Minor in Slavic Languages and Literatures
Requirements: The minor in Slavic Languages and Literatures requires seven courses beyond the first-year language sequence in the primary language of study, including at least three language courses at the 20000 level or higher and at least one course in Slavic literature, culture, or linguistics. [2] Students who elect the minor program must meet with the Departmental Adviser before the end of Spring Quarter of their third year to declare their intention to complete the minor and must submit a signed Minor Consent Form to their College adviser. [2, 7] Courses in the minor may not be double counted with the student's major(s) or with other minors and may not be counted toward general education requirements. [2] Courses for the minor must be taken for quality grades. [2]
Department: The College, Division of the Humanities, Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Sociology
Requirements: The University of Chicago requires applicants to submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, which includes a personal essay. In addition, applicants must answer the UChicago Supplement questions, which include a choice of creative essay prompts. [2, 3] Other requirements include a secondary school report and transcript, and two teacher recommendations. [2] The university values a strong high school academic record with coursework in English, mathematics, social sciences, and laboratory science. [3] Submitting SAT or ACT scores is optional. [8, 10] An optional two-minute video introduction can also be submitted in place of a traditional interview. [8]

ProgramName: Minor in Sociology
Requirements: Information for a 'Minor in Sociology' is not available on the official The University of Chicago website. The university's general process for minors involves declaration by already-enrolled undergraduate students, not a separate application. Specific application documents are not required.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in South Asian Languages and Civilizations
Requirements: The University of Chicago uses a holistic application review process for all undergraduate programs, including the Bachelor of Arts in South Asian Languages and Civilizations. While there are no specific application requirements for this major beyond the general requirements for The College, students who are admitted and choose to major in South Asian Languages and Civilizations must complete a two-quarter South Asia civilization sequence and achieve proficiency in a South Asian language equivalent to at least one year of study. [1, 14]
Department: Department of South Asian Languages and Civilizations, Humanities Collegiate Division

ProgramName: Minor in South Asian Languages and Civilizations
Description: The minor program in South Asian Languages and Civilizations requires a total of six or seven courses, depending on whether the sequence SALC 20100-20200 Introduction to the Civilizations of South Asia I-II or two quarters of the SOSC 23004-23005 South Asian Civilizations in India I-II sequence taught in Pune are used to meet the general education requirement or to meet the minor program. [2] All students in the minor are required to take two quarters of SALC 20100-20200 Introduction to the Civilizations of South Asia I-II or SOSC 19016-19017-19018 South Asian Civilizations in India I-II-III (taught in Pune). [4] These two quarters will count toward either the general education requirement in civilization studies or the minor itself. [4] If SALC 20100-20200 or SOSC 23004-23005 are not used to meet the general education requirement, both courses in the sequence must be included in the minor, for a total of seven courses. [2, 4] Students pursuing a minor in South Asian Languages and Civilizations must take a quality grade in all courses used to meet department requirements and more than half of the requirements must be met by courses bearing University of Chicago course numbers. [2, 4]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Statistics
Requirements: Application for admission to the Bachelor of Arts in Statistics is made through the general undergraduate admissions process at the University of Chicago, using either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. There are no separate application requirements specific to the Statistics major. General requirements include the application form, supplemental essays (including a 'Why UChicago?' essay), letters of recommendation, and high school transcripts. The university does not specify program-specific requirements for the BA in Statistics at the undergraduate application stage.
Description: Mathematics a ținut întotdeauna un rol major în toate domeniile statisticii, de la teoria probabilităților la analiza datelor. Statistica este un domeniu potrivit pentru studenții cu abilități matematice și de calcul solide și cu un interes în aplicarea acestor abilități la probleme din științele naturale și sociale. Un program care duce la obținerea diplomei de licență în Statistică oferă o acoperire a principiilor și metodelor statisticii în combinație cu o pregătire solidă în matematică și calcul. Specializarea poate oferi o pregătire adecvată pentru studii postuniversitare în statistică sau în alte domenii cu componente cantitative puternice. [6]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Statistics
Requirements: Applicants apply to the University of Chicago through the Common Application or Coalition Application. General requirements include a strong high school academic record with recommended coursework in English, mathematics, laboratory sciences, social sciences, and a foreign language. [3, 15] The application includes the UChicago Supplement, which features a required extended essay known as the "Uncommon Essay," and requires two letters of recommendation from teachers in academic subjects. [2, 18]
Description: The modern science of statistics involves the development of principles and methods for modeling uncertainty; for designing experiments, surveys, and observational programs; and for analyzing and interpreting empirical data. Mathematics plays a major role in all areas of statistics, from probability theory to data analysis. Statistics is an appropriate field for students with strong mathematical and computational skills and an interest in applying these skills to problems in the natural and social sciences. A program leading to the bachelor's degree in Statistics offers coverage of the principles and methods of statistics in combination with solid training in mathematics and computation. The major can provide appropriate preparation for graduate study in statistics or in other subjects with strong quantitative components. Students considering graduate study in statistics or related fields are encouraged to discuss their programs with the Departmental Adviser for Majors at an early stage, whether or not they plan to receive an undergraduate degree in Statistics.

ProgramName: Minor in Statistics
Fees: $71,325 per year for the 2025-2026 academic year. [15]
Description: The minor in Statistics requires five courses, some prescribed and some elective, chosen in consultation with the Departmental Adviser for Minors. [2] It is designed to complement degree programs in computer science, economics, and the social and natural sciences. [4] The modern science of statistics involves developing principles and methods for modeling uncertainty, designing experiments, surveys, and observational programs, and for analyzing and interpreting empirical data. [2] Mathematics is a major component of all areas of statistics. [2]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit awards start at $2,000. The First Phoenix Scholarship provides $20,000 over four years. [13]
ScholarshipType: Merit-based scholarships are available to all first-year applicants based on academic and extracurricular achievements, leadership, and community commitment. [13, 14]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Theater and Performance Studies
Description: Theater and Performance Studies (TAPS) seeks to animate the intersection of theory and practice in the arts. The program is comparative in multiple ways, requiring its students to acquire facility in the practice of two media (e.g., theater, film, video, dance, music, creative writing) while gaining fluency in the critical analysis of those media. To this end, a student majoring in TAPS receives training in both performance practice and analysis, acquiring the fundamental skills for artistic creation while developing a nuanced and sophisticated vocabulary for analyzing creativity. In this way, the program aims to contest the ready separation of academic theory and artistic practice or, for that matter, of theorists and practitioners. The program is designed to be flexible (to afford students as much latitude as possible in pursuing their particular interests) and exacting (to guarantee the development of comparative practical skills and rigorous analytic capacities).

ProgramName: Minor in Theater and Performance Studies
Requirements: Students who elect the minor program must meet with the Director of Undergraduate Studies before the end of Spring Quarter of their third year to declare their intention to complete the minor. [2] Students should file a Worksheet to the Minor form with the Director of Undergraduate Studies by the beginning of Spring Quarter in their third year, and the signed form must be submitted to the student's College adviser. [4] The TAPS minor requires a total of six courses plus a public performance of original work (e.g., staged reading, site specific installation, solo performance piece, choreography). [2] Courses in the minor may not be double counted with the student's major(s) or with other minors and may not be counted toward general education requirements. [2]
ScholarshipAmount: Merit-based scholarships start at $2,000 and can be for full tuition. [15]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Tutorial Studies
Bachelor of Arts in Visual Arts
Minor in Visual Arts
Department: The College, Division of the Humanities, Department of Visual Arts
Description: The minor in visual arts requires six courses: one is from the 10000-level sequence (ARTV 10100 Visual Language: On Images, ARTV 10200 Visual Language: On Objects, or ARTV 10300 Visual Language: On Time and Space), and five are drawn from visual arts studio courses numbered 21000 to 29700, chosen in consultation with the Director of Undergraduate Studies. ARTV courses numbered 20000 to 20999 are not studio-based and are generally not counted toward studio requirements for the minor. [1]

ProgramName: Minor in Yiddish
Requirements: A combination of six language and literature/culture courses are required for the minor. [2] Students who elect the minor program in Yiddish Studies must meet with the program administrator before the end of Spring Quarter of their third year to declare their intention to complete the minor and must submit the Consent to Complete a Minor Program form to their College adviser. [2]
Description: Students in any field may complete a minor in Yiddish Studies. A combination of six language and literature/culture courses are required for the minor, which should be designed in consultation with the program coordinator. [6] Courses in the minor may not be double-counted with the student's major(s) or with other minors, and may not be counted toward general education requirements. [6] Courses in the minor must be taken for quality grades, and more than half of the requirements for the minor must be met by registering for courses bearing University of Chicago course numbers. [6]
